utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. This is Wednesday, the 2nd of May, 2007. I'd like to greet everyone here in the courtroom. I'd like to greet Mr. Scott, who has come back with us. I would like to say good afternoon to Mr. Poryvaev as well, and good afternoon to the Defence counsel and to the accused, as well to everyone present in this courtroom. The cross-examination of the witness will continue with Mr. Karnavas, Mr. Karnavas who has been offered some time by other Defence teams, if I'm not mistaken. Mr. Karnavas, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I believe I have in total 30 minutes. I thought it was 40, but in any event it will be 30 minutes, 10 for myself and then I believe 20 from Ms. Alaburic, and then that should be enough. Again, good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yesterday you talked a little bit about the radio station in Mostar, and I believe you indicated in your testimony yesterday, this would be on page 8, line 3, that it was -- the name was changed to Croatian Radio Station, and again that also can be found in your statement that you gave back in 2002. So is it your testimony, sir, that the name of the station was changed to Croatian Radio Station Mostar or Croatian Radio Mostar? That's your testimony; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did change its name into Croatian Radio Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Very well. Now, we saw some documents yesterday. I won't go through those documents again, but they -- I leave it for the Trial Chamber to look and see what the title of the station is, but let's look at document 1D 01418. Sir, we're going to have to move rather quickly now. 1D 01418. This is dated December 4, 1992. Again, we can see the names. We have Muslim names. We don't know whether they're actually Muslim or not, but they're Muslim names. But at the top we see that it's the radio of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and the title is Radio Station Mostar. Do you see that, sir? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you repeat that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear the number or couldn't follow the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. It's 1418. 1418. It would be 1D 01418.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. It says at the top Radio Station Mostar. Does it not say that, sir? It's a yes or no.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. And in fact we can also see the salaries and it would appear that everybody's receiving the same amount; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says on this piece of paper. There's no doubt that that is what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. If we could go down to the next -- if we could go to the next document, and this is a -- P 00486. P 00486. Again, this is dealing with the name, and it fits within -- within the theme of this particular cross-examination, which is embellishment. If we look at this, this is a decision, sir, is it not, dated 21 May 1992, and there in this decision we see it's the radio -- the radio of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, Radio Station Mostar.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says the radio station of the Croatian Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unless I'm very much mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But it doesn't say Croatian Radio Station, does it? And --

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Croatian Defence Council is not the Muslim Defence council.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir. Sir, sir. I'm going to cut you off here. That's why we went through the names, to point out that there were Muslims working in the radio station. You said that the name of the station was -- just listen to the question. You said that the name of the station was changed to Croatian --

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And here we see that it's called Radio Station Mostar; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I didn't have an insight into official documents. I just know how they addressed themselves, Croatian Radio Station Mostar. That was the official title on the air. But I have a question for you. Do you know how long these people worked there and who is working at that radio station now?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir. We're not on one of your talk shows. Here you listen to questions and you answer them. Okay?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Okay. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I want to apologise and correct the record. It's 16 September, 1992, Your Honours. You'll see that at the end, at the bottom of the page where it says Friday, 16 September 1992. I misspoke.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: What month is rujan, September; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now if we could go on to the next topic, again dealing with the radio -- Radio Mostar. If we could look at 1D 01421. 1421. And let me apologise, sir, if I appear rude. I'm just short of time. I wish we could have time to debate. Now, if we could look at this document --

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry. I'm sorry we don't have the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay, if you could look at the document 1421, it's dated December 21, 1992, at the top we see Radio Mostar. This is a memo. At the bottom we see that there's a -- it's signed by head imam of the committee Sefko Efendi Tinjak, I believe. Do you recognise this individual?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And here if we -- if we look in -- we don't have much time to spend on this document, but we would see in the second paragraph at the very last line it talks about alongside this, "We think it would be desirable if you would give us two hours a week of air time during which we would introduce Islam to the people." And if we had the time to go through the previous paragraphs, you would see that the imam wishes to air for the Muslims an Islamic programme because of the upcoming fasting period. And that's all I need for this document. And again it's addressed as Radio Mostar, for the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that Radio Mostar of Herceg-Bosna or some other Radio Mostar? Because this radio station, Radio Mostar, as such did not exist in this form.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: So could you tell me?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, was there another Radio Mostar operating in -- in -- in Mostar at the time?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was Croatian Radio Mostar and Radio Bosnia-Herzegovina War Studio Mostar. Those two stations existed --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: --- And if you look at the documents --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Do you think that the imam would know the difference of the two and would know how to address them? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I assume he would, but perhaps he didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Very well.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well f we could look at 1D 01419. This is from Faruk Cupina. You know this gentleman, don't you? At the end of the -- 1419. Faruk, Faruk Cupina. You know -- you know the gentleman; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And here again this is dated December 24, 1992, and it appears, at least from the first paragraph under "Dear sirs," it says, "We would like to use this occasion to inform you that the Executive Committee of the council of Muslims of Herzegovina held a meeting on December 23rd, 1992, and concluded among other things the following," and it would appear that this is something that is being presented to Radio Mostar in order for this to be publicised. Would that be correct or am I misreading this document, or maybe you can't answer the question.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether Radio Mostar received this, whether it broadcast it, but I just see that it says Radio Mostar and that's a station I'm -- I don't know about, because that kind of station didn't exist, but I assume Cupina knows what he sent to whom. But a radio station under that name did not exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And then we have another document and it's dated 1420 [sic]. 1420. Dated December 31st, 1992. And if we look at it, it actually -- it almost -- it almost dovetails the letter that we first saw, which was dated December 21st, because it then goes on to say at the bottom in the text that a meeting was held and that they would agree to air -- to have air time every Thursday during the fourth daily sala [phoen] and on Fridays from 12.00 to 12.45 during the Dzuma namaz. Okay? And so to your knowledge you don't know what radio station they're referring to when it says here Radio Mostar?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Very well. Now, I want to switch to another topic. Yesterday, as I understand it, you indicated that at one point you had worked for a newspaper called Mostar Morning; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostarsko Jutro, that's what it was called, Mostarsko Jutro, meaning "Mostar morning."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And you worked for that publication?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I wrote a few articles for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And that publication was actually operational during the year 1992, was it not? Yes, no, maybe, I don't know?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it came out in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And that was a -- that paper was controlled or operated by Muslims, was it not?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say that. The paper was the paper of the 1st Mostar Brigade, and in the Mostar Brigade you had all nationalities, all ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Okay.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: So I don't know what you mean when you say Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So was it controlled by the ABiH? Is that what you're telling me? The army of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Sir --

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the publisher was the 1st Mostar Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, under whose control that was, I don't know. There was no control. It was -- well, it was -- probably somebody had to provide the money for the publication.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And the 1st Mostar Brigade was under the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna or was it under --

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, no, it wasn't. I was a member of the 1st Mostar Brigade but I was never a member of --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... under. Who was it part of? What -- that was a unit of what? Of the army of BiH?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The First Independent Autonomous Mostar Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. And I next only because -- and we're going to go through some of these documents because in your statement in 2004 you said that in 1992 all Croatian papers were available in Mostar, and it would appear at least where I come from that that statement would be less than honest or less than correct?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostarsko Jutro wasn't sold. It was distributed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could buy --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- those publications that came from Zagreb, for instance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we -- if we could go to 1D 01422. 1D 01422. This is a -- a copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And we don't have the exact dates, Your Honour. We're going to try to find the original ones, but from the text we can glean that this was -- this would have been published on or about 27 August 1992. You could see on the left bottom corner the logo, but the reason I say that this would have been published at or about because this article relates to conclusions based on an agreement at the meeting in Medjugorje.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, does this look like incidentally, sir, does this look like what the -- this publication was like at the time? Is this -- does this appear to be a copy of Mostar Morning, the publication that you indicated you worked for at one point or contributed to?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wrote a few texts for the Mostar Morning, but I wasn't on the editorial board. I don't know if this is the Mostar Morning. It's kind of a customary page that you would find in any newspaper.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If you look at the logo, on the left side, bottom page. Do you see it?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I see something black, but it doesn't resemble a logo to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm short of the time. I don't want to debate with the gentleman, but I do wish -- I do wish for the Trial Chamber to take into consideration the gentleman's demeanour and his willingness or unwillingness to be candid with the Court because the oath says the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. And incidentally one other matter, Your Honour, with respect to the particular agreement being referenced here, this has been introduced under P 00339. It's the agreement on friendship and cooperation, so that's what's being referred to in this particular document when they talk about the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we could look at the next document, 1D 01424. Again, this is -- it would appear that this is from the same publication. I would venture to say that it's on or about November 9 because we could see that both at the top and in the very first sentence. And again, if you look at the left side, bottom of the left side on the original copy, you'll see a stamp. There may not be a logo, but it certainly is a stamp. And we don't have the time to go through this, but do you recall reading this at all? Yes, no, maybe, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The stamp that you said was a stamp, in one place you called it a logo and in the other you say it's a stamp. But it's the same thing. So what do you take me for? It's the same thing. You said it was a logo here and you said that it's a stamp there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- work on the logo for the Mostar morning, so I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's why I don't want to argue with you. Does this appear -- do you know who Mr. Jaganjac, Jasmin Jaganjac was? Do you know him? Do you know him sir, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know Arif Pasalic, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you recall reading anything about --

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Do you recall reading anything about the events that are outlined in this particular article?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Very well. 1D 01423.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Again, we'll discuss this through other witnesses, Your Honour, but this is the vehicle that -- this is the individual who is the vehicle to get these documents in. And again on the left side of the bottom page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Karnavas, I have a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: How do you know in 10 seconds the witness knows what the contents of an article is?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Because this was so celebrated of an incident, that is the agreement between the two sides, and all he needs to do is read the headlines. I'm willing to give the gentleman time, but, you see, I'm caught between not having time by the Trial Chamber because of the rush to do things and the gentleman who obviously would need time to read it. And so I'm -- that's the dilemma that I'm in. Under normal circumstances I would spend two or three hours with this gentleman. I don't have that luxury. But the point that I'm trying to establish here, Your Honour, is that these are publications that were published at the time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- and to get them in. And then later, you know, the Trial Chamber will have the benefit through other witnesses, perhaps. I don't want to debate what the actual content --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Well, I just have to note that the time for me is too short to know what this is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, if we could go to one last -- one last document. Okay. I'm told I haven't finished with 1D 01423. Again, do you see at the bottom of the left side that it says Mostar Morning in your language? Does it say that? It's a stamp. It's a logo. I don't know what it is but something that's designated on the very first page, on the left side at the bottom. All of them have the same. I just want you to say it for the record, do you see it? Yes or no. If you don't see it, that's fine. Can you read it? You can turn the page a little bit. If you need your reading glasses we'll go get them. Can you read it, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'll move on, Your Honour, because I don't have time.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters are having difficulty to following the speed of the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's not a logo. You keep mentioning this logo. It doesn't resemble a logo. It says "Mostarsko Jutro," but it could say --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas and the witness, the interpreters have troubles following you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I say something, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry, we don't have the time. If we could go on to P 00946.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can't insult me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No one is insulting you, sir, but you need to answer questions here. That's what you -- you were brought here. And yesterday you had no problems answering the questions of the Prosecution. Now if we could look at P 00946.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I just mention this, Your Honour, because this goes -- this is put into context with the previous documents because they relate to -- you don't have this document in front of you but this is for the Court's benefit that this document would have been already introduced but this goes with this packet of material as well because you will see it relates to a commission that was set up between Mr. Boban and Alija Izetbegovic, where Mr. Boban appoints Zoran Buntic, Anto Valenta, and himself. And then it Mr. Izetbegovic appoints Mr. Trnka, Mrs. Salakovic, and another individual's name to be on the commission. And this again goes to the joint commission that was referenced in the first article that I mentioned 1D 01422.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we could go on to another section now, and if we look at 1D 01215. 1D 01215. This is --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We've seen this document before, Your Honours. That is a decree on carrying out control of information during a state of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Were you aware of this decree, sir, that came out of the Sarajevo government? 5 September 1992. You were a journalist at the time. I assume you kept a -- you kept abreast of the legislation that controlled your -- your profession. Were you aware of this decree on carrying out control of information during state of war? Yes or no or I don't recall?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know about that decision, and it was impossible to have any contacts with Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: We couldn't get anything from Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Based on this -- on this decree, Your Honours, you will see that in Article 2 it talks about, "control shall be applied to all types of information, verbal, written," and so on and so forth, issued by the armed forces. I point this out because now I want to go -- I would like to go into private session just to cover one document to perhaps show some linkage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, may I just ask, I presume you will propose to take this to -- to submit this document as evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: What is the link to the witness who says he's never seen it and doesn't know about it and did not say that, you know, anything about what the ruling was?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Before -- we've had a journalist here before, and -- and that journalist who was with the Muslim army or the Muslim fighters at the time indicated how he had to get pre-clearance in showing foreign journalists around because everything was being monitored and censored as it were. Here we have a law that pretty much says so. Now, this gentleman may not be aware of it, but nonetheless it is something that was in existence. Now, I have another document, which I would like to go into private session, which perhaps may assist in the linkage of this. And that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just one thing I want to ask you about, your apartment, because we have a document you indicated yesterday that at some point you lost the key -- the keys to your apartment that was on the west side that was 500 to a thousand metres from the Vranica building that you were evicted basically. That's what you were -- and that it wasn't until two or three years ago that you got your apartment back. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't lose them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, the witness did not say he lost them. They were taken away from him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: It's not the same Mr. Karnavas in law. You know quite well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, it's a figure of speech.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Well, you are yourself very critical of figures of speech on the other side, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, if you just let me do my cross, you'll see I'm going to get there step-by-step.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But with that clarification, you -- you indicated that you lost your apartment back in 1993; correct? And it wasn't until two or three years ago that you got it back. Do you recall saying that yesterday?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is what I stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, we have documents that we've introduced before and they come under a bundle of 3D 00734, and in these -- in this document there are several lists of names that were provided by Arif Pasalic for certain individuals to get certain apartments that would have been made available as a result of the JNA having to leave and these apartments being vacant. And so Arif Pasalic made a request of the HVO that certain individuals who qualified under certain conditions, such as somebody who might have been injured, a soldier who might have been injured, would qualify. And I notice that under number 663.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: This would be at the second to last page, Your Honours. It's number 15. It's the second to last page of the bundle.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Under 663 it appears that it has somebody's name there that looks very familiar or similar to yours. Is that your name, sir?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: What page is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: For you -- if you would look at those -- at the top of the page, it's 03270574.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Or plain 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Or 15. At the very -- it's at the end. Second to last page. Second to last page of this particular document. You see -- you'll see -- yeah, okay. So go down to 663. Do you see 663?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, could you assist us here? It's so elementary I don't understand what the problem is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just bear with me for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm trying. I just don't have the time and you're taking forever.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry you don't have the time. Yes, I've got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, is that your name, sir?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is my name.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now -- so when we're talking about the apartment, is this an apartment on the west side that you obtained as a result of Mr. Arif Pasalic's request of the HVO or was this an apartment that you had prior to the incident, prior to the events?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Prior to the events.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: This has nothing to do with anything whatsoever. This is the first time I see this piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Can I ask if you already had an apartment where you and your wife and your children were living in --

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Why -- okay. Okay. If you had that, then why would -- Arif Pasalic would be also making a request --

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm just asking the question. Maybe he knows. Maybe he doesn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: The witness said -- just as stated, that he'd never seen the document. What is the relevance?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I didn't ask him whether he saw the document because he may have made a request. Maybe he wanted a larger apartment. Maybe Arif Pasalic was just confabulating himself, just putting down names so they could get more and more apartments because that's what they were trying to do, move people into the west side. I don't know. I'm merely asking the gentleman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir, you don't have to look at the Prosecutor and motion to him. Okay? So the question is --

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: My question is: Did you know that Arif Pasalic had put your name down for an apartment?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know. I've never seen this before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know. I've never seen this before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay, and -- and, of course, one last question. Based on your testimony, there was no need for you to have an apartment at that because you already had one and therefore if this request is made by Arif Pasalic then obviously it might have been for other reasons?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: That's pure speculation and even insulting the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's not insulting but it is speculation. But I mean, it drives the point home. And the point is, what fits into this -- into our theory, that there's a whole lot of propaganda going on and there's a whole lot of events happening, including trying to obtain apartments for individuals who already have apartments and don't need apartments. And that's what I was trying to drive at. I have no further questions for the gentleman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you very much. One follow-up question, sir. You've stated on many occasions that the radio station where you worked was in the Vranica building at the same level or on the same floor as the office of Mr. Pasalic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. If I may compare things, and I'm sorry if I'm making this comparison, it's a little bit like if in Baghdad the CNN station was situated a few metres away from the headquarters of the American troops, for instance. So an observer from the outside may wonder what is the possible connection between the reporters and the soldiers within the headquarters especially since you yourself mentioned that you were a member of the ABiH. Your radio station, therefore, was it functioning under the ABiH control or did you have a complete freedom, total freedom to -- did you have an editorial freedom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The radio station had complete freedom. The fact that it was located in the area of the command of the 1st Mostar Brigade in the 4th Corps did not condition its programmes. It was not dictated by the army or anybody from the army. All those who listened to our programmes can confirm that the army did not edit the radio programmes. I was the link between the radio and the 4th Corps, as I was a member of that corps. At that time no programme ranging from a simple piece of news too reports from the front lines, and when I say reports from the front lines I would say what the situation was like and this was the only thing that was subject to censorship. But this is something that I did within the command. This was information that was available to everybody and boiled down to some ten sentences in any one day. The radio station programmes were intended for all the citizens of Mostar for them to hear things that they could not hear on radio Herceg-Bosna. Today in Mostar there is Radio Mostar, Croatian Radio Mostar. There is also the radio of Herceg-Bosna, but when you look at the context then it might appear the fact. However, if we had broadcast from any other part of the town I don't think that we would have been able to survive because it was very dangerous.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My colleague has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I would like to ask you a question with regard to the name of the radio station. The Defence counsel asked you some questions and he showed you some documents, and in -- we did not see in any document that the radio station was called the Croatian Radio of Mostar. However, we see Radio Station Mostar in all documents. Even if I must recognise that in the document 1D 01416, the first sentence reads as follows: [In English] [Microphone not activated] We attach the list of employees of the PEICM radio of the Croatian Defence Council, Radio Station Mostar." [Interpretation] So, are you saying that there's absolutely no document on which we can see the official name Croatian Radio Mostar, but it was only the of staff and the authorities of that radio who would call it Radio Mostar. Is that what you're telling us, that no document actually bears that name, radio Croatian -- Croatian Radio of Mostar? Can you confirm that to us?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation] This could not be changed by judicial order. I know that on air we would always say that this was the -- Croatian Radio Mostar. I don't know whether officially it was named just Radio Mostar. I know that this is what was repeated, Radio Mostar in the second part. I never had an opportunity to see whether this was officially Radio Mostar, the Croatian Radio Mostar, the Radio Herceg-Bosna, or the radio of the Croatian Defence Council. In this document I can see that this was the radio of the Croatian Defence Council. That's one radio. In the second document when they received the second salary, then they were called the Radio Herceg-Bosna. Just for comparison there is another -- a radio today in Mostar which is called radio Herceg-Bosna, but this is not an old radio station. It was set up some seven or eight years ago. I did not see any documents, but I know that the announcement on air was always Croatian Radio, Radio Mostar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A follow-up question from my colleague. When the Defence counsel showed you these documents we were under the impression that you never -- that you did not know that radio station, whereas these documents show there were at least 15 people out of which three reporters, sound technicians as well, and these people were paid by that radio station. That radio station in question with -- when we talk about the media, we always listen to the competitor's radio station. You never tried yourself to listen to Radio Mostar of Herceg-Bosna just to see what their programme was like?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course I listened to that. I know these people. Under number 3, here, is one of my best friends. However, Your Honours, people, as the counsel has put it rightly, I don't know whether there were Muslims or not. It is not up to me to say whether somebody was Muslim or not. Their name might be Muslim, but an interesting thing is that Asim Manjgo who was one of the founders of the war radio station was an employee of this radio. There are also Serbs who worked for the radio who are not on the list. I knew all of them. As for the Muslim name, these people remained there only for a short while. They were just a facade, and none of them have remained working for the radio. And the programmes that they broadcast reflected exactly what I was talking about. Croatian radio was allergic to the notion of Bosnia and Herzegovina. This was a constant thing on the radio. It couldn't happen that somebody from the leadership of the army or the civilian structure came to the radio as the counsel put it, those who bore Muslim names. Look at the editors at the radio. They wore uniforms, and it says in the documents that it was the radio of the Croatian Defence Council. I was a member of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and never pledged loyalty to the HVO. When we were offered to do so, all of us who refused to sign that pledge fared the way we did. I listened to the radio. I know very well what their music was like and what they said on the radio.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next counsel, Ms. Nozica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... may I just -- may I just make one statement to the Trial Chamber. He just indicated that he knew the third person on the list, and I just wish to bring that to the Court's attention yesterday he was playing games with the Court as to whether the names were Muslim or not. I just wish to point that out. And also I wish to point out to the Trial Chamber that yesterday he talked about being the editor of the information and propaganda service within the -- and today he said he wasn't. I just thought this is something -- it betrays the gentleman earnestness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Who is this third person on the list? It's Veseljko Cerkez. Is that the person you knew?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Veseljko Cerkez. Veseljko Cerkez. My colleague, a journalist. The counsel asked me yesterday whether they are Muslims. I don't know. Only God himself knows whether they believe in him. In the document that I saw before stated that I was the editor-in-chief of the radio but I wasn't. I was the editor of the information programme. I'm just saying this to bring this point home. If the counsel wants to play with words, I'm game.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Lizde?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I have handed over the binder for the Trial Chamber. I would kindly ask the registrar to provide both the Prosecutor and the witness with their binders. You don't have to consult my binder at the moment. I'm going to ask you a few questions. There are not many documents in that binder anyway, so I believe we will be able to go over them very fast. Mr. Lizde, you have just mentioned some things that have inspired me to put a certain number of questions and we're talking about the negative propaganda that was spread by the media in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I'm sure that you will agree with me when I say that such negative propaganda was present on all three sides and -- am I right in saying that? Having said that, I have in mind the Serbian radio stations, the Croatian radio stations, and the radio stations that existed in the areas under the control of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is very likely that you're right in saying that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I would like to hear your explanation. Yesterday you said that you had worked for Radio Sarajevo, a radio station of Mostar. Was that the official title?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: What was it then?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the question -- the answer? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Radio Bosnia and Herzegovina, the War Studio Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did this war studio continue operating after the 9th of May when the antenna was destroyed? It could not continue operating in the Vranica building.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It continued operating in another part of the town after the 9th of May conflict. I was no longer there. I know it continued its operation, but I don't know when this happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You said that you edited the political programmes and everything that had to do with the army and information about the BiH army. Can you remember whether you heard information being published about the situation on the front line and the word used for Croats was Ustasha or some other derogatory words. Maybe not by yourself personally but some guests that arrived at the station.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't use those words. I don't think that any of my guests used them. I don't think that we resorted to that level because I'm sure that we would have faced problems. We tried and I was the editor of the political programme and I had a lot of guests. We tried to not to add fuel to the fire that already was burning in the town. So I'm very positive that such things did not happen, and I'm talking about the period preceding the 9th of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: The reason that you have just mentioned why you didn't do it, was it because the radio was located at the heart of the western part of Mostar? Was that the reason?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't the reason, but from this perspective when you look at the things as they were, the political situation, the relationship between the army and the HVO and everything that we heard from Sarajevo, that there had been a military putsch in Sarajevo and the Croatian people did not depend on Sarajevo but on Zagreb, in Mostar an alibi was being prepared all the time for what would happen later on, and I'm sure that any such situation would have been used in their favour. For example, Juka's of -- from Sarajevo was one such situation and various incidents in Mostar. We Bosniaks all -- were always under the impression that an alibi was being sought for something that had already been prepared but the implementation was still questionable. But this is still the situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you. You have mentioned Juka's arrival. You say -- you've said that you're sorry that we don't have more time. You've mentioned Juka's arrival. Can you please tell me -- can we confirm that he was one of the prominent members of the BH army in Sarajevo, that he was a general in Sarajevo, that he was one of the people next to Alija Izetbegovic at the beginning of aggression in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what Juka was elsewhere. I know what he was in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So you don't know.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know. I was not in Sarajevo at that time. I only heard what he was in Sarajevo. I've read about that. I've read a lot of things. But I know what he was in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let's now move on to another topic. On page 4, just for the transcript, you don't have to peruse your documents, I'll remind you -- I have not provided you with your statement. On page 4 in the Croatian version of your statement, and in the English version it is page 3 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Ms. Nozica, page 4 of what, which document?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could you please bear with me just for a moment. I will -- all shall be revealed at the end. We're talking about the statement of this witness dated 10 and 12 April and 7 and 12 June 1992. I'm referring to page 4 of that statement in the Croatian version and page 3, paragraph 3 in the English version of the same statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: In that statement you stated, Mr. Lizde, that you had been in Prozor on the 20th of October, 1992. Yesterday, you told us on your direct examination that this was on the 21st. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could have been either 20th or 21st. I can't -- I can't be sure. I might have been off by a day. It was on one of the two days but it was in Prozor. I'm sure of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Lizde, you've also told us that Mr. Dzidic brought a decision on the ban of the operation of the war radio of Mostar on the 21st or the 22nd of October, 1992. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was one day after my return from Prozor, in any case.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You have left us these two days as possible days for your stay in Mostar, so for example if you were there on the 20th and the decision was made on the 21st or if you were in Prozor on the 21st and the decision was made on the 22nd. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Lizde could you please confirm something that I will paraphrase as what you saw in Prozor? You've told us that you saw torched houses.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I saw some houses that were on fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You said that you did not see any civilians, but you had learnt that they had been taken away to the school in Ruboka [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The troops that I spoke to told me that the civilians had been taken to Rumboci, which is a place next to Prozor.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Rumboci. That's right for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that you were told that by members of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You also said that you saw a white sheet on the fire brigade where it says Ustaski Dom; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You said that the HVO soldiers who were standing in front of this Dom building, that there was no longer any Turkish zulum there in Prozor, no Turkish clout.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: When did you leave Mostar?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: We left in the morning, came back in the evening, and we had an hour to talk. That was the permission we were given by the commander who talked to us for some five minutes in front of his HQ.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can we say that you in fact saw the consequence of that HVO military action in Prozor immediately after it happened?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes that would be it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you tell me, Mr. Lizde, and I think that -- well, you're a journalist first and foremost so that applies intelligence and all the rest of it. Why Bozo Rajic and Srecko Vucina told you or gave permission to go to Prozor if they knew that the HVO had done such a terrible thing in Mostar -- I'm sorry, I misspoke, in Prozor. Why would they give you that permission? Did they perhaps not know that it had happened, or did they not have anything to hide? What did you think about that?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't believe that they thought that there was anybody as mad as that to go there, but there were a lot of problems, and I'm sorry that you don't have an insight into the press conferences that were held before and after, because they were real arguments. We had real arguments at those press conferences.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Would you concentrate on my questions?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. They weren't uninformed about what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Lizde, can we see when these things happened in Prozor and look at document P 00629? It is in the pink binder, my pink binder. 629 is the document number. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you and I agree that this is the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and that it is a document signed by the head of the brigade, Petar Kolakusic; is that right? And can you see the date of the document?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document is dated the 23rd.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: The 23rd of October. Let's read the first sentence. It says "report." As it was over 24 hours and it says, "around 1500 hours heavy clashes between our forces and the OSBH," that is to say the armed forces of BH. And the pretext, the reason was that the units from Gornji Vakuf at the border of Prozor municipality and Gornji Vakuf and the sabotage unit at elevation 1030 killed two of our soldiers. Two were less seriously wounded. A number of prisoners were taken. The situation is under control. It is controlled by our police forces and army. From this document it would appear that what happened in Prozor occurred on the 23rd of October at around 1500 hours.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about this. I don't think we're talking about same document. I know that the conflicts in Prozor lasted for a very long time. Now, this conflict with the BH army that this document talks about, well, I never said that the BH army had a conflict with the HVO. The soldiers told me that they had cleared the area and burnt houses. Now they would have bragged had they taken a lot of the members of the armed forces prisoner. I don't know when the conflicts began in Prozor. I was in Prozor.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now on the basis of this document there were conflicts in Prozor?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think these were the initial conflicts.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Just a moment. I understand your nervousness.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not nervous at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Well, that's your reaction. You either didn't see what you've been describing happen in Prozor because -- I'm just going to tell you this once and won't dwell on it I'm going to say it for the Trial Chamber and refer to the indictment and count 46 of the indictment, or paragraph 46 where it says in the afternoon hours of the 23rd of October, 1992, the forces of Herceg-Bosna, the HVO, attacked the Muslims in the town of Prozor. On the 23rd -- between the 23rd -- on the 23rd and 24th of October, 1992, after they had taken control of Prozor town, the Herceg-Bosna forces plundered, burnt, and destroyed homes, et cetera. That's what it says in the indictment. Paragraph 46, sir. So then what you say as being an event of the 20th and possibly the 21st of October, in fact never happened in Prozor. Let's move on to another area, another topic. You said in your statement, and you repeated that today in answer to Mr. Karnavas, and you've just repeated it again in response to Judge Mindua, that you were not within the frameworks -- when you joined the BH army in April that that was not within the frameworks of the HVO, is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I did not sign an oath of allegiance in joining the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you tell me when you joined the Mostar Battalion? When was that, what month?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Regardless of whether you sign the joining up agreement or not, and you insist you were never in the HVO, I assume that's important to you, but can you tell me if it's true and correct whether the Mostar Battalion was within the municipal headquarters of the HVO of Mostar? When you joined the Mostar Battalion, was it part of that at the time?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Do you know or can I confirm that the Mostar Battalion at the time, and we're talking about April when you joined up -- I see that you're distracted by my documents.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I'm not. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Although Judge Prandler didn't have his microphone on, I understood what he was telling us. So I do apologise and we will slow down, and I'll repeat my question.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: But wait a moment. I'm speaking as fast as you. So if I'm going to slow down, then you slow down, too, and make pauses between my questions and your answers, because quite obviously everybody has a problem, the Judges, the interpreters, and everybody. So let me repeat my question. When you joined up, when you joined the Mostar Battalion, do you know whether it was in the composition of the Municipal Staff of the HVO Mostar?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was within its composition but I do know that there was a number of joint common elements because with the Mostar Battalion and the company that I was with, I went to Goranci, and up there for the first 10 or 15 days we spent there we received food from the HVO, from their logistics, and then a piece of paper arrived for us to join -- to sign the piece of paper saying -- pledging our allegiance, and we didn't do that. That's what I know. So you can't actually say that at the beginning the answer would be yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. That's what I wanted to hear. So you know without a doubt that in April the Mostar Battalion was part and parcel of the HVO. Without going into the documents, do you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay, okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, I'll take you back for a moment to the -- your arrest of the -- on the 9th of May. When you were in the MUP building you said that an incident took place that somebody -- some of the detainees were mistreated and that this was intensified when a man called Lugonja was killed.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that. He was wearing a flak jacket.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Was he an HVO member?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that he was well-positioned, a well-positioned policeman.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: A member of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, the HVO, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Tell me, please, how did he die?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he was hit by a sniper.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did you know, Mr. Lizde -- well, you've talked quite a lot about the snipers from the Croatian side. Did you know at the time that the BH army in Mostar had snipers, sniper shooters, and do you know in what locations?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea what you're talking about. I don't know. I was in the MUP building when the man was hit. I assume he wasn't hit by a shell, a hand grenade.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You said he was hit by a sniper.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a sniper hit him underneath flak jacket. Where the sniper came and who shot at him, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I didn't ask you that.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: You asked me about the army. It was a real army and it had a sniper.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Don't take that turn. There's no need for that. Just answer my question. So it had sniper shooters in Mostar. Can we put it that way?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that. You said that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let's not play around with words.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you're playing around with words.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You yourself said that the BH army had sniper shooters, had snipers, and that was on page 36, line 7, and you said that it was a real army. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely so.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Right. Then we can move on. Mr. Lizde, yesterday my colleague Mr. Ibrisimovic showed you a document, and I'd like to show it on e-court for just a moment. It is 6D -- it will come up on your screen. 6D 00349 is the document number. Now, I'll remind you while the -- you're waiting for the document. It is the head of the human rights and humanitarian issues department attached to the office of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. You'll remember that I'm sure, and you referred to it. I'm going to focus on a paragraph, paragraph 2 or, rather, paragraph 3 in the English version, and yesterday you reacted to that where it says despite the findings of the investigation confirmed by the statements of the persons mentioned which indicate activities contrary to professional work and professional code of conduct of journalists, the authorities of the HZ HB decided to release you, to set you at liberty. Now, Mr. Lizde, did you have any information to the effect that with respect to your activities an investigation was conducted?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't have that information. There was -- were daily interviews, and I assume they had a purpose.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Right. Fine. And did you have information that a criminal report was filed against you?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can we take a look at the next document and it is a Prosecution document to boot, so in the preparation the Prosecutor could have shown you the document. It is P 08508. It is the last document. It's a rather lengthy one, but we'll start from the beginning. It is a criminal report filed by the crime department of the military police, military post. 1706 is the number on the 21st of December, 1994. Yes, the first page. The criminal report was filed on the 21st of December, 1994. So you can leaf through it and look at point 249. In the Croatian version it is on page 12, and in the English version it is on page 11. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Have you found your name there?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Right. Fine. So a criminal report was filed against you, too, and I'll just tell you that you'll be able to find this at the end on page 20 of the Croatian version and page 18 of the English version. And from this it would emerge that the criminal report was filed against 400 known perpetrators and 12 unknown perpetrators. From this criminal report we can see it was filed, and I say this for the record because there was a well-founded suspicion that the individuals had committed a war crime against the civilian population pursuant to Article 142 of the war crimes against injured persons and six -- sick people. Article 143. And war crimes against prisoners of war pursuant to Article 144. Organised groups for the inciting of war crimes pursuant to Article 145. And in citing an aggressive war pursuant to Article 152, taken over from the Criminal Code of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. So I've just shown you this document for you to see that your interviews and what you said resulted in the filing of this criminal report with the District Military Court in Mostar, and you said that you knew nothing about this.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. Fine.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they showed some goodwill and released me.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: That's what it says in the document.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I can well believe that. Can you?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'm just showing you the document and showing you what it says there. It's a document that we received from the Prosecution, so it is not something which I'm showing you because I have any ill intentions.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can see all the members of the BH army on that list. The whole Mostar Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very likely. But I'm not going to look at the other members for my purpose. Just wanted to look at your name there but thank you, Mr. Lizde. That completes my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Before we move on we'll have a 20-minute break because the time has come for the break, and we'll resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just for your information, I would like to say that General Praljak has 35 minutes, and 35 minutes have been given to him by Mr. Pusic, which makes it a total 65 minutes. I would like to start, and then Mr. Praljak will finish off at the end of my cross-examination. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So who is starting, you or Mr. Praljak, because Mr. Praljak is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak will --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. My mic was not working. If I have to repeat, Mr. Praljak will start and I will have 10 minutes on the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I'm going to object with the points the Prosecution has raised over the last few weeks. No showing or proffer has been made as to why it is appropriate for Mr. Praljak to put questions to this witness, how this is an exceptional circumstance based on purely technical military basis. So we object to Mr. Praljak putting any questions to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I have to respond, although I don't deem this is necessary, I believe that the accused Praljak has the right to defend himself and represent himself. The rules allow that. You have pointed it out on several occasions. His questions do not have to be limited to technical details although he will adhere to that. And third of all, when it comes to the facts, this is not a legal matter, and the accused is perfectly capable of putting questions. The accused is not an object of the proceedings but, rather, a subject of the proceedings, and he is entitled to take an active part in the proceedings irrespective of who the witness may be.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: We stand by our objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I just want to tell the parties --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Honourable Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. This issue has been raised several times. The Chamber has heard the views of both parties and a decision on this matter is in preparation and will be rendered in short time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I just -- because it's been commented before that I have not preserved objection, I just want to be very careful from now on until there is a clear and firm and fixed ruling on the matter that I will -- I have -- we do object, and we'll have a continuing objection to Mr. Praljak participating without the requisite showing having been made by the outstanding ruling on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, so that Mr. Scott is not under that obligation, I think I raised the point about whether that had been waived. I -- I can absolve Mr. Scott from any further obligation to makes the objection. It's understood that he makes it. My point was not that he's making objections now but that a year had gone by in trial during which time the accused had been permitted to cross-examine in person, and my point was it was now too late to change that. But Mr. Scott shouldn't feel it's necessary to make an objection certainly for my sake every time that it's raised from now on. I'm not going to take that point against him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, you've listened to this discussion. Please try to deal with technical issues when putting your questions to the witness, and there might be a number of technical issues to be raised here because we are dealing with a former member of the ABiH, after all.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Accused Praljak. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Cross-examination by the Accused Praljak:

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Lizde was member of the BiH army. He was wounded. He wore a uniform, and in that sense I don't see why I should not discuss with him some military matters very calmly in order to establish some facts. Mr. Lizde, I have designed my questions in such a way that enables you to answer them either by I know, I don't know, and avoid comments that might distract anybody. You have already talked to the Prosecutor. You have provided your comments, and I'm just going to go through some parts of the time from 1992 onwards, and I'm going to ask you whether you're aware of some facts. If you are, then just say yes. If not, then just say no. Would you agree with me that the Yugoslav People's Army and the reservists already before 1992 but certainly in April 1992 were on Hum and on the other hills around Mostar on the right bank and the left bank of Mostar, Hum, Decici, Slipcici on the right bank; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Praljak. This is something that was not covered by -- in direct examination, which does not exclude it, but you have asked a leading question and you should not do that. That's a rule that has now been accepted here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may present my view. The questions pertaining to this domain are relevant and have to do with the existence of the joint criminal enterprise that could not have emerged in space. It had to emerge within the circumstances that prevailed on the ground specified as the beginning of the events in Bosnia, and this time is specified in the indictment. As for your second remark, I believe that it is a rule in the Rules of Evidence that talks about the cross-examination of witnesses which allows the Defence to present their case to the witness. In other words, that they may ask questions based not only on what was used in the cross, which is the rule in the Anglo-Saxon law, but can also use the witness if the witness has any knowledge about things by presenting their defence case to the witness. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Karnavas. I have not said that this was not a subject on which questions could be put, but I recall that we have had a discussion on this matter before. The rule is specified in the American law, I admit, but it's a good rule. When the Defence in cross-examination wants to go beyond the field that was covered in direct, it is actually using the witness as the Defence's witness. That is possible. But the same rule as for another direct examination must apply. That is to say the question should not be a leading question. We have had this before here, and I remember very well that Mr. Karnavas, after first having protested that there was not -- no such rule, later on expressly accepted that this was the rule. It is a rule that makes a lot of sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- I do recall that we had the discussion about Rule 90(H) and the scope of cross-examination. I must confess that I'd forgotten the part about the leading questions. Your Honour, from -- from memory, I think there's something of a division among American jurisdictions. Some -- some do adhere -- adhere to the point that Your Honour makes and others allow the cross-examination simply to cover the ground without distinguishing between leading and non-leading questions. So I think there is that decision. In English law I'm very confident about saying that any question in cross-examination may be put in either leading or non-leading form regardless of whether it -- it flows from direct examination or not. So that's my understanding. I'll be corrected if I'm wrong. That's my understanding about the domestic law. As far as the law of the Tribunal is concerned, which would be controlling, I think Your Honour may have the advantage of me and may have read something that I haven't. I am not aware of a decision that has the effect that Your Honour describes, but if Your Honour would like to point -- to draw it to my attention perhaps I can look at it and give Your Honour more complete assistance on another occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't claim to be the ultimate authority --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Just, just.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: As I was invoked, I think it is section 711 or 611 of the American code of civil procedure, and it's expressly in a code. It's not a matter of dispute or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour is exactly right. It is Rule 611. The point I was making, though, I think Your Honour is probably looking at the federal rules of evidence. Your Honour may know that in the United States there are the federal rules but then there are also state rules of evidence that apply in the state individually. While there is obviously a broad similarity between the rules there is in fact a division of authority between the federal model and other models. So in many jurisdictions Your Honour is absolutely right, but it's not an invariable rule. And in England I'm very confident in saying. But I think the rule point is what's the law in the Tribunal. I'm not aware of any direct authority and I don't think it's covered in any of the rules, but Your Honour may -- knows of a decision that I'm not familiar with on that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- I was just going to say I don't claim the ultimate authority, but my understanding in English law is exactly the same as --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I thought my microphone was working. Is it not? Yes. Yes, my understanding of English law is exactly the same as Mr. Murphy's. Your Honour Judge Trechsel gave the American rule as described and said it was a good rule. Your Honours, with respect, that must rather be open to debate. We don't always sail the English system is the best, but the fact that we adopt a different practice does at least raise the possibility that there's room for two arguments on that issue, and simply to assert that it is a good rule may be pre-empting the result of what might need to be a rather fuller argument on the topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I have not just asserted, Mr. Stewart, I have given the reason for it. I have given the reason for it. Because it is -- there is no justification for the Defence going into a new terrain on a technique which is not allowed on direct but only on cross. But let me add that at any way, answers to leading questions are of little evidentiary value. So the rule in fact goes in favour of the Defence, but it's a matter of technique. I do not want to insist now. Maybe the Chamber will make a ruling on this and I think we'll let go. Now, I'm a bit disappointed I must say that the Defence now suddenly raises this issue again.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I say, because Your Honour makes the point just -- Your Honour says you don't just assert that you give the reason. After all, I'm not here with a brief of English law but it's unlikely that the practice and the rules have been developed in English law without realising that the reason Your Honour puts forward is one the arguments. It's not -- We're not so unsophisticated that we don't take accounts of those matters, and also, Your Honour, it's a matter for judgement of the cross-examiner. Your Honour is absolutely right, and any skilled cross-examiner, experienced cross-examiner knows that sometimes it's better not to extract answers by absolutely directly leading questions because if you get them another way they can be of more value. But that is conventionally left the judgement of the cross-examiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't want to prolong the discussion of course as Your Honour knows I'm always delighted when the Trial Chamber is prepared to adopt rules of evidence. I would -- I would suggest that perhaps the rule that governs here may be sub-rule (F) of Rule 90 which says that the Trial Chamber shall exercise the mode and role of interrogating witnesses so as to make the presentation effective for the presentation of truth and avoid needless consumption of time. I think that's also taken from another American rule with a little variation, and I would suggest that in the absence of a definite rule on this point in Rule 90 it may be that it's up to the Trial Chamber to -- to control the mode of interrogation in the particular case. The only point I'd make on that, if Your Honour is going to allow Mr. Praljak as a layman to cross-examine it may be perhaps more fair to him not to insist too much upon the form of the question. Your Honour, those are the only submissions. If Your Honour would like me to brief it more fully at a later time I would be happy to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I just wanted to raise an objection to the record that I don't subscribe to the notion that answers to leading questions are of little evidentiary value.
